text: Everything so far runs because you explicitly called it. A trigger is different — it's code that fires automatically whenever a table changes, with no explicit call at all. This lesson covers the AFTER trigger, which runs once the triggering change has already happened.

Create trigger trg underscore Product underscore PriceAudit, on Production dot Product, after update. Inside, an INSERT into an audit table, selecting from inserted joined to deleted on product ID, keeping only rows where the price actually changed. One trigger definition covers insert, update, and delete together if you list all three after AFTER.

Inside any trigger, SQL Server hands you two automatic pseudo-tables. Inserted holds the new values — populated on insert, and on update. Deleted holds the old values — populated on delete, and on update. An update is the interesting case: it populates both, which is exactly how that audit trigger captures an old price and a new price with one join.

Here's the part that matters: an AFTER trigger runs inside the same transaction as the statement that fired it, before that transaction commits. So if the trigger body finds a problem — say, a negative price — and issues ROLLBACK TRANSACTION, the entire original update is undone, not just whatever the trigger itself was doing.
Next lesson covers the other kind of trigger — one that doesn't run after the change, but instead of it entirely.
